claim: Normal genomic DNA contains hundreds of mismatches that are generated daily by the spontaneous deamination of C (U/G) and methyl-C (T/G).
source: 'Normal' genomic DNA contains hundreds of mismatches that are generated daily by the spontaneous deamination of C (U/G) and methyl-C (T/G).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established scientific knowledge about DNA chemistry and is referenced in the manuscript (Barnes and Lindahl, 2004).

claim: Mismatches introduced into human cells on an SV40-based episome were invariably repaired.
source: We show here that while mismatches introduced into human cells on an SV40-based episome were invariably repaired, this process induced mutations in flanking DNA at a significantly higher rate than no mismatch controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically Figure 2B showing repair outcomes.

claim: Repair of mismatches introduced into human cells on an SV40-based episome induced mutations in flanking DNA at a significantly higher rate than no mismatch controls.
source: We show here that while mismatches introduced into human cells on an SV40-based episome were invariably repaired, this process induced mutations in flanking DNA at a significantly higher rate than no mismatch controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A with statistical analysis (p-values).

claim: Most mutations induced by mismatch repair involved the C of TpC, the substrate of some single strand-specific APOBEC cytidine deaminases.
source: Most mutations involved the C of TpC, the substrate of some single strand-specific APOBEC cytidine deaminases, similar to the mutations that can typify the 'mutator phenotype' of numerous tumors.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 4, demonstrating the dinucleotide context of mutations.

claim: TpC preferring APOBECs mediate the mutagenesis induced by mismatch repair.
source: siRNA knockdowns and chromatin immunoprecipitation showed that TpC preferring APOBECs mediate the mutagenesis
evidence: This claim is supported by siRNA knockdown experiments (Figure 6A) and ChIP experiments (Figure 6C).

claim: Both the base excision and mismatch repair pathways are involved in generating mutations during mismatch repair.
source: siRNA knockdowns showed that both the base excision and mismatch repair pathways are involved.
evidence: This claim is supported by siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: The spontaneous deamination of C and methyl-C daily generates hundreds of U/G and T/G mismatches respectively.
source: For example, the susceptibility of C (and its methylated derivative) to spontaneous hydrolytic deamination daily generates hundreds of U/G and T/G mismatches respectively, (Barnes and Lindahl, 2004)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Barnes and Lindahl, 2004.

claim: C is the most frequent source of single nucleotide substitutions in mammals.
source: could explain why C is the most frequent source of single nucleotide substitutions in mammals (Hwang and Green, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hwang and Green, 2004.

claim: Error-free base excision repair (BER) can correct the naturally occurring U/G and T/G mismatches.
source: Error-free base excision repair (BER) can correct the naturally occurring U/G and T/G mismatches (reviewed in Cortázar et al., 2007; Hegde et al., 2008; Robertson, 2009; Jacobs and Schar, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to review articles.

claim: In lymphoid (B) cells, U/Gs generated by activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID) are prone to several mutagenic processes that enhance diversification of immunoglobulins.
source: However, in lymphoid (B) cells the U/Gs that are generated by activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID, a member of the AID/apolipoprotein B mRNA editing enzyme, catalytic polypeptide-like (APOBEC) family of cytidine deaminases, Conticello, 2008) on transient single-stranded DNA regions produced during transcription, are prone to several mutagenic processes that enhance diversification of immunoglobulins (somatic hypermutation, SHM, Martomo and Gearhart, 2006; Teng and Papavasiliou, 2007; Peled et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to the literature on somatic hypermutation.

claim: MMR is a high fidelity process that operates post-replicatively on the nascent DNA strand to remove mismatches that have escaped the proof-reading activity of high fidelity replicative DNA polymerases.
source: Normally, MMR (Modrich, 2006; Hsieh and Yamane, 2008; Jiricny, 2013) is a high fidelity process that operates post-replicatively on the nascent DNA strand to remove mismatches that have escaped the proof-reading activity of high fidelity replicative DNA polymerases.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to reviews on mismatch repair.

claim: In B cells, non-canonical MMR can expose single stranded regions at U/G-containing sites unrelated to DNA replication that can serve as a template for DNA repair.
source: In B cells, non-canonical MMR can expose single stranded regions at U/G-containing sites unrelated to DNA replication that can serve as a template for DNA repair.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the literature on non-canonical MMR in B cells.

claim: The high fidelity DNA polymerase is replaced by the error-prone polymerase η in B cells during non-canonical MMR.
source: However, the high fidelity DNA polymerase is replaced by the error-prone polymerase η (mediated by mono-ubiquitylated PCNA).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about somatic hypermutation mechanisms.

claim: Extracts of non-lymphoid mammalian cells can process U/G mismatches by a non-canonical MMR process.
source: Recently, elements of non-canonical MMR have been recapitulated in vitro (Schanz et al., 2009; Peña-Diaz et al., 2012), and the latter study also showed that extracts of non-lymphoid mammalian cells can also process U/G mismatches by a non-canonical MMR process.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Peña-Diaz et al., 2012.

claim: Non-lymphoid cells when stressed in vivo by the alkylating agent MNNG generated more mutations in MMR proficient than deficient cells.
source: In addition, these non-lymphoid cells when stressed in vivo by the alkylating agent, N-methyl-N′-nitro-N-nitrosoguanidine (MNNG), generated more mutations in MMR proficient than deficient cells, thereby implicating MMR in the mutagenic process but presumably using an AID-independent mechanism (Hsieh, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hsieh, 2012.

claim: The high mutation rates of the C of TpCpN (or its complement, G of NpGpA) can accompany the progression of some cancers.
source: Recent examples of such a mutator phenotype are the high mutation rates of the C of TpCpN (or its complement, G of NpGpA) that can accompany the progression of some cancers (Nik-Zainal et al., 2012; Roberts et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to cancer genomics studies.

claim: TpC-preferring members of the AID/APOBEC family of C deaminases, particularly APOBEC3B, mediate mutations in some cancers.
source: TpC-preferring members of the AID/APOBEC family of C deaminases, particularly APOBEC3B (A3B), mediate these mutations (Burns et al., 2013; Leonard et al., 2013; Roberts et al., 2013; Taylor et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to cancer genomics studies.

claim: Transitory single stranded regions that arise at replication forks or during double strand break repair can accumulate mutations upon chronic alkylation of DNA.
source: Experiments using yeast as a model system showed that the transitory single stranded regions that arise at replication forks or during double strand break repair can accumulate such mutations upon chronic alkylation of DNA (Roberts et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Roberts et al., 2012.

claim: Mutations were observed at experimentally introduced double strand breaks coincident with overexpression of AID/APOBEC deaminases.
source: These mutations were also observed at experimentally introduced double strand breaks coincident with overexpression of AID/APOBEC deaminases (Taylor et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Taylor et al., 2013.

claim: Processing lesions harbored by SV40 episomes faithfully captured the DNA repair repertoire and mutational environment of its host.
source: Numerous studies have shown that processing lesions harbored by such episomes (as well as those introduced in the SV40 virion) faithfully captured the DNA repair repertoire and mutational environment of its host (e.g., Hare and Taylor, 1985; Seidman et al., 1985; Brown and Jiricny, 1987; Choi and Pfeifer, 2005; Terai et al., 2010; Pathania et al., 2011; Qi et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies using SV40 episomes.

claim: The introduced mispairs were invariably corrected when episomes were passed through mammalian cells.
source: We found that the introduced mispairs were invariably corrected.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 2B showing repair outcomes.

claim: Repair of introduced mispairs generated mutations in normal flanking DNA at statistically higher rates than the no mismatch control, but only if the episomes were passed through mammalian cells.
source: However, their repair generated mutations in normal flanking DNA at statistically higher rates than the no mismatch control, but only if the episomes were passed through mammalian cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 2A and the statement that no mutated episomes were obtained if passed directly into E. coli.

claim: Most of the mutations involved the C of TpCpN, regardless of the lesion type.
source: Regardless of the lesion, most of the mutations involved the C of TpCpN, and shared other features of the aforementioned mutations that occur in some cancers.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 3D showing dinucleotide context of mutations.

claim: siRNA knockdowns showed that the TpC-preferring deaminases, particularly A3B mediated the mutagenic effect.
source: siRNA knockdowns showed that the TpC-preferring deaminases, particularly A3B mediated the mutagenic effect
evidence: This claim is supported by siRNA knockdown data in Figure 6A.

claim: Chromatin immunoprecipitation showed that A3B could access the episome in a mismatch dependent way.
source: chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) showed that A3B could access the episome in a mismatch dependent way.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP data in Figure 6C.

claim: siRNA knockdowns showed that components of both the BER and MMR pathways are involved in generating the single-stranded APOBEC substrate.
source: siRNA knockdowns also showed that components of both the BER and MMR pathways are involved in generating the single-stranded APOBEC substrate
evidence: This claim is supported by siRNA knockdown data in Figure 8.

claim: ATR and PCNA modulate the mutagenic effect of mismatch repair.
source: two factors that have diverse roles in various aspects of DNA metabolism, ataxia telangiectasia and Rad3-related protein (ATR) and PCNA (Moldovan et al., 2007; Flynn and Zou, 2011) modulate the mutagenic effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by siRNA knockdown data in Figure 9.

claim: APOBEC deaminases are relatively ubiquitous in various tissues.
source: The APOBEC deaminases are relatively ubiquitous in various tissues (Refsland et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Refsland et al., 2010.

claim: Repair of different types of mismatches or lesions (T/G, 5-hydroxymethyl-U/G, U/G, or an abasic site opposite a G) induced significantly more mutations in the reporter region than the 0 MM control.
source: Figure 2A shows that the repair of different types of mismatches or lesions - T/G, 5-hydroxymethyl-U (hmU)/G, U/G, or an abasic site opposite a G, (ab)/G – induced significantly more mutations in the reporter region than we found with the 0 MM control.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A with statistical significance indicated.

claim: HmU is a byproduct of the enzymatic demethylation of methyl-C.
source: HmU is a byproduct of the enzymatic demethylation of methyl-C (Bhutani et al., 2011; Guo et al., 2011; Wu and Zhang, 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on DNA demethylation.

claim: Abasic sites are generated during BER.
source: abasic sites are generated during BER (e.g., Robertson, 2009; Jacobs and Schar, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to reviews on base excision repair.

claim: No mutated episomes were obtained if they were passed directly into E. coli.
source: Finally, no mutated episomes were obtained if they were passed directly into E. coli (3 deleted episomes /42,000 colonies screened, results not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data (though not shown in figures).

claim: Repair of top strand T/Gs generated approximately fourfold more mutated episomes than the 0 MM control.
source: Thus, more deaminase is bound to the supF reporter of top strand U/G- than bottom strand U/G-containing episomes (cf. mutational frequencies in Figure 2, panel C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 2A showing mutation frequencies.

claim: HmU/G repair induced approximately sevenfold more mutations than the 0 MM control.
source: HmU/G repair induced ∼sevenfold more mutations (0.182%)
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 2A.

claim: U/G or ab/G repair induced approximately 30-fold more mutations than the 0 MM control.
source: U/G or ab/G repair induced ∼30-fold more mutations (0.726% and 0.78% respectively) than the 0 MM control.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 2A.

claim: The bottom strand location reduced the mutagenic effect of repairing U/G or ab/G, but not of T/G or hmU/G.
source: The bottom strand location reduced the mutagenic effect of repairing U/G or ab/G, but not of T/G or hmU/G.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 2A comparing top and bottom strand lesions.

claim: Repair of bottom strand T/G was approximately twofold more mutagenic than on the top strand.
source: Repair of bottom strand T/G was ∼twofold more mutagenic than on the top strand: 0.23% ± 0.013 vs 0.11% ± 0.011 (mean ± standard error, p<10−7, Fisher exact test).
evidence: This claim is supported by data with statistical analysis.

claim: Except for T/G, essentially all of the top and bottom strand lesions were restored to C/G.
source: Figure 2B shows that, except for T/G, essentially all of the top and bottom strand lesions were restored to C/G.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 2B.

claim: T/G was converted to T/A about 25% of the time.
source: T/G was converted to T/A about 25% of the time.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 2B.

claim: The ratio of restoring T/G to C/G or converting it to T/A was independent of repair-induced mutagenesis.
source: Thus, the ratio of restoring T/G to C/G or converting it to T/A was independent of repair-induced mutagenesis.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of repair outcomes in mutated vs non-mutated episomes.

claim: Conversion of T/G mismatches to T/A had been observed with T/G-containing SV40 virion DNA.
source: Conversion of T/G mismatches to T/A had also been observed with T/G-containing SV40 virion DNA (e.g., Hare and Taylor, 1985; Brown and Jiricny, 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The mutagenic effect was independent of the G+C content of the mismatch region.
source: The mutagenic effect was also independent of the G+C content of the mismatch region; 69% G+C for FM1, 39% for FM2, and 53% for FM3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The distance between the cis 3′ end of the reporter region and the lesion affects mutagenesis.
source: The distance between the cis 3′ end of the reporter region and the lesion is <50 bp for top-strand, but ∼5 kb for bottom-strand lesions in FM1 (top panel Figure 2C). This difference accounts for their different mutagenic effects
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 2C showing different episome configurations.

claim: Relocating the MM region upstream of the reporter region switches the mutagenic effects of top and bottom strand lesions.
source: because relocating the MM region upstream of the reporter region (M1F) switches these distances (now <50 bp for bottom—but ∼5 kb for top-strand lesions respectively), and it also switches the extent of their respective mutagenic effects (cf. top and middle panels of Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 2C.

claim: Reversing the orientation of the entire reporter cassette has the same effect on mutagenesis as relocating the MM region.
source: Reversing the orientation of the entire reporter cassette (the DNA between the EcoRI and NheI sites [Figure 1A] to produce FM1_R [Figure 2C, lower panel]) has the same effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 2C.

claim: Strand-specific mutagenesis is neither due to transcription nor DNA replication effects imposed on the reporter region by the episome backbone.
source: These results also show that strand-specific mutagenesis is neither due to transcription nor DNA replication effects (i.e., transcribed vs non-transcribed strand, and leading vs lagging strand, e.g., Fijalkowska et al., 1998; Hanawalt and Spivak, 2008) imposed on the reporter region by the episome backbone.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the episome orientation experiments and supported by citations.

claim: BER would be recruited to T/G, hmU/G and U/G mismatches.
source: BER would be recruited to T/G, hmU/G and U/G mismatches (Robertson, 2009; Jacobs and Schar, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to reviews on DNA repair pathways.

claim: A preformed SSB can induce mutagenesis in flanking DNA.
source: The most right hand bar graphs in the upper and middle panels in Figure 2C also show that a preformed SSB (i.e., one did not result from BER activity on the introduced mismatches) can also induce mutagenesis in flanking DNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 2C.

claim: The preformed SSB <50 bp from the cis 3′ end of the reporter region generates the same mutagenic effect as U/G-ab/G at these positions.
source: The preformed SSB <50 bp from the cis 3′ end of the reporter region in the top strand of FM1 or bottom strand of M1F generates the same mutagenic effect as U/G-ab/G at these positions.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 2C.

claim: Processing a nick bypasses T/G repair and generates a substrate that is susceptible to mutagenesis.
source: Therefore, processing this nick bypasses T/G repair, and generates a substrate that is susceptible to mutagenesis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from data in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: A preformed SSB at approximately 5 kb from the cis 3′ end of the reporter region has little if any mutagenic effect.
source: However, unlike the other lesions, a preformed SSB at ∼5 kb from the cis 3′ end of the reporter region (bottom and top strand respectively for FM1 and M1F) has little if any mutagenic effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 2C.

claim: The mutations are distributed throughout the cassette, mostly on G, irrespective of the type of lesion.
source: The mutations are distributed throughout the cassette, mostly on G, irrespective of the type of lesion (summarized in Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 3A, 3B, and 3C.

claim: The sequence context of approximately 80% of the G mutations is GpA, but with less specificity for the 5′ base.
source: In addition, the sequence context of ∼80% of the G mutations is GpA, but with less specificity for the 5′ base (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 3D.

claim: Essentially the same mutational spectrum was induced by restoring each type of top strand lesion to C/G.
source: Figure 3—figure supplement 1 shows that essentially the same mutational spectrum was induced by restoring each type of top strand lesion—that is, T/G, hmU/G, U/G or ab/G to C/G.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: A similar mutagenic process is recruited during repair of any of the lesions (T/G, hmU/G, U/G or ab/G).
source: Thus a similar mutagenic process is recruited during repair of any of these lesions.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the similarity of mutational spectra shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The preponderance of mutations on the G of GpA indicates that its complement on the repair template, the C of TpC, is targeted by the mutagenic process.
source: The restoration of top strand lesions to C/G would employ the bottom strand as the repair template. Thus, the preponderance of mutations on the G of GpA indicates that its complement on the repair template, the C of TpC, is targeted by the mutagenic process that is recruited during repair.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the mutational data and the repair mechanism.

claim: The preference for mutations at the C of TpC implicates the TpC-preferring APOBEC family members of single strand-specific cytidine deaminases.
source: This preference implicates the TpC-preferring APOBEC family members of single strand-specific cytidine deaminases.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the mutational signature and knowledge of APOBEC substrate specificity.

claim: The most frequent mutational outcome at GpA was a G to A transition.
source: The fact that the most frequent mutational outcome at GpA was a G to A transition is consistent with the above two mechanism of generating an A opposite the original C of TpC (Figure 4B, upper left quadrant).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 4B.

claim: Replication across the abasic site by various other DNA polymerases could insert a T or C opposite the abasic site and generate G to T or C transversions.
source: On the other hand, replication across the abasic site by various other DNA polymerases could insert a T or C opposite the abasic site and generate G to T or C transversions (Lange et al., 2011), which we also found (Figure 4B, upper left quadrant).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 4B and citation to Lange et al., 2011.

claim: Approximately equal amounts of transitions and transversions result from repair-induced mutagenesis.
source: As a consequence approximately equal amounts of transitions and transversions result from repair-induced mutagenesis, an outcome that was also observed for APOBEC-mediated mutations in some tumors (Burns et al., 2013; Leonard et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 4B and citations to cancer studies.

claim: When bottom strand lesions are restored to C/G, most of the mutations are on C of TpC.
source: Now, most of the mutations are on C of TpC when the lesions are restored to C/G (Figure 3—figure supplement 4)
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: The most common mutational outcome for bottom strand lesions restored to C/G involves C to T transitions with about an equal amount of transversions to A and G.
source: as the lower left quadrant of Figure 4B shows, the most common mutational outcome involves C to T transitions and with about an equal amount of transversions, to A and G.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 4B.

claim: When a top strand T paired with a bottom strand G is converted to T/A, most of the mutations are on C.
source: Thus, when a top strand T paired with a bottom strand G is converted to T/A, most of the mutations are on C (Figure 3C, T/G_con)
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 3C.

claim: Approximately 80% of mutations when top strand T/G is converted to T/A involve the C of TpC with almost no specificity for the 3′ base.
source: ∼80% of which involve the C of TpC with almost no specificity for the 3′ base (top panel, Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: When a bottom strand T/G is converted to T/A, most mutations are on the G of GpA.
source: However, when a bottom strand T/G is converted to T/A, most mutations are on the G of GpA (Figure 3—figure supplement 3–T/G_con, Figure 3—figure supplement 5, bottom panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and 5.

claim: Approximately equal amounts of G and C mutations are generated from the 0 MM controls.
source: Approximately, equal amounts of G and C mutations are generated from the 0 MM controls (most left hand bar graphs, Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The mutational spectra from 0 MM controls resemble what would result from repair of a mixture of top and bottom SSBs.
source: These mutational spectra and their dinucleotide sequence contexts resemble what would result from repair of a mixture of top and bottom SSBs (Figure 3—figure supplement 6, Figure 3—figure supplement 7)
evidence: This claim is inferred from comparison of mutational spectra.

claim: The trinucleotide context of about half of the G mutations was ApGpA.
source: Although the trinucleotide context of about half of our G mutations was ApGpA, the others were mostly CpGpA and not TpGpA
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 8.

claim: The APOBECs do not strongly discriminate between the nucleotides that are 3′ to TpC.
source: These results indicate that the APOBECs do not strongly discriminate between the nucleotides that are 3′ to TpC (readily apparent in Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the mutational data.

claim: A lack of discrimination on 3′ nucleotides was shown in vitro for APOBEC3B.
source: A lack of discrimination on 3′ nucleotides was also shown in vitro for APOBEC3B (Burns et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Burns et al., 2013.

claim: Mutations can occur in a concerted fashion in 25-30% of the episomes.
source: Thus, mutations can occur in a concerted fashion, which is the case for 25–30% of the episomes (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: The mutational spectra and dinucleotide contexts of clustered and unclustered mutations induced by repair of top strand lesions did not differ.
source: This figure also shows that the mutational spectra and the dinucleotide contexts of the clustered and unclustered mutations induced by repair of top strand lesions did not differ
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: All clustered and unclustered mutations from top strand lesions exhibited the mutational preference for the complement of the C of TpC, that is, the G of GpA.
source: and all exhibited the mutational preference for the complement of the C of TpC, that is, the G of GpA.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 5B.

claim: The spectra and dinucleotide context of clustered and unclustered mutations induced by repair of bottom strand lesions differed.
source: However, the spectra and dinucleotide context of clustered and unclustered mutations induced by repair of bottom strand lesions differed.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: Clustered mutations from bottom strand lesions had the same mutational APOBEC signature as the top strand lesions.
source: In contrast to the clustered mutations, which had the same mutational APOBEC signature as the top strand lesions (Figure 5B)
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 5B.

claim: Unclustered mutations from bottom strand lesions show less of a preference towards mutating the C of TpC.
source: the unclustered mutations show less of a preference towards mutating the C of TpC, most evident for those induced by restoration of T/G to C/G (cf. lower 2 panels, Figure 5A and the lower panels labeled unclustered, Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: Several APOBEC deaminases, including A3B, A3F and A3C are expressed in HeLa cells.
source: qRT-PCR (Refsland et al., 2010; Burns et al., 2013) showed that several APOBEC deaminases, including A3B, A3F and A3C (Conticello et al., 2007; Prochnow et al., 2009) are expressed in the HeLa cells (HeLa_JM)
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 7A.

claim: A3B, A3F, and A3C exhibit >40% preference for TpC.
source: A3B, A3F, and A3C exhibit >40% preference for TpC (Bishop et al., 2004; Langlois et al., 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on APOBEC substrate specificity.

claim: siRNA directed at A3B, A3F, and A3C reduced their expression.
source: Figure 6A shows that siRNA directed at them reduced their expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 6A.

claim: Knockdown of any one of A3B, A3F, or A3C marginally affected the mutational frequency.
source: While knockdown of any one of them marginally affected the mutational frequency
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 6A.

claim: Knockdown of two deaminases (A3B and A3F) inhibited mutagenesis associated with T/G and U/G repair.
source: knockdown of two (A3B and A3F) inhibited mutagenesis associated with T/G and U/G repair (middle panel, Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 6A.

claim: Knocking down all three deaminases (A3B, A3F, and A3C) eliminates the mutational signature associated with deamination of the C of TpC.
source: the lower part of Figure 6A shows that only knocking down all three deaminases (siA3(B,F,C)) eliminates the mutational signature associated with deamination of the C of TpC.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 6A.

claim: Single knockdowns of A3B, A3F, or A3C change the mutational signature with respect to the dinucleotide context consistent with the extent of their preferences for TpC.
source: However, even though the single knockdowns did not substantially inhibit the mutational frequency, they do change the mutational signature with respect of the dinucleotide context (hereafter referred to as the dinucleotide signature) consistent with the extent of their preferences for TpC (Bishop et al., 2004; Langlois et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 6A and citations.

claim: Knocking down A3C (46% preference for TpC) hardly alters the dinucleotide signature.
source: Thus, knocking down A3C (46% preference for TpC) hardly alters the dinucleotide signature
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 6A.

claim: Knocking down A3B (91% preference for TpC) had a more profound effect on the dinucleotide signature.
source: whereas knocking down A3B (91% preference) had a more profound effect
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 6A.

claim: The knockdown of A3F (77% preference for TpC) produced an intermediate effect on the dinucleotide signature.
source: and the knockdown of A3F (intermediate at 77%) produced an intermediate effect on this signature.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 6A.

claim: The three deaminases (A3B, A3F, A3C) compete for substrates generated during repair.
source: these data suggest that while the three deaminases compete for substrates generated during repair
evidence: This claim is inferred from the knockdown data.

claim: A3B is the most important contributor to repair-induced mutagenesis.
source: A3B is the most important contributor to repair-induced mutagenesis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the knockdown and rescue data in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: Expression of siRNA-resistant A3B reversed the mutagenic effect of the triple knockdown of A3B, A3F and A3C.
source: Expression of hemagglutinin (HA)-tagged A3B, which is resistant to siA3B (top panel, see 'Materials and methods') reversed the mutagenic effect of the triple knockdown of A3B, A3F and A3C (siA3(B,F,C), middle panel)
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 6B.

claim: Expression of siRNA-resistant A3B restored the TpC mutational signature.
source: and restored the TpC mutational signature, but not if it lacked deaminase activity, A3B_Cat (bottom panel, Figure 6B
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 6B.

claim: Catalytically inactive A3B does not restore the TpC mutational signature.
source: but not if it lacked deaminase activity, A3B_Cat (bottom panel, Figure 6B

source: Thus, U/G repair was about fivefold more mutagenic in HeLa_JM than in HEK293 although their APOBEC repertoires were comparable.

source: Therefore, factors other than just the availability of these deaminases are required for repair-induced mutagenesis, in agreement with observations on some cancer cells (Roberts et al., 2013).

source: This result is consistent with a model whereby MMR can not only highjack BER intermediates generated from a T/G mismatch but also directly access the mismatch, that is, independently of BER.

claim: Direct access of T/G by MMR has been demonstrated in vitro.
source: Direct access of T/G by MMR has been demonstrated in vitro (Pluciennik et al., 2010; Peña-Diaz et al., 2012).

source: The knockdown of neither BER nor MMR affected the mutational signature of induced mutagenesis (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).

claim: BER and MMR pathways act upstream of the APOBEC deaminases.
source: Thus, these pathways act upstream of the APOBEC deaminases.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the fact that knockdowns don't affect mutational signature.

source: Inhibiting PCNA synthesis somewhat reduced T/G-induced mutagenesis

source: but ATR knockdown had no effect.

source: In contrast, PCNA knockdown stimulated the mutagenic effect of U/G repair

claim: ATR knockdown inhibited the mutagenic effect of U/G repair.
source: but ATR knockdown inhibited its effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 9A.

source: Figure 9C shows that the kinase activity of ATR is essential for its effect on U/G-repair-induced mutagenesis

source: and further corroborates the siATR knockdown, because ATR deficient in kinase activity does not rescue it.

claim: Neither PCNA nor ATR knockdown altered the mutational signature of repair-induced mutagenesis.

source: Thus, similar to the BER and MMR proteins, PCNA and ATR act upstream of the APOBEC deaminases.

claim: APOBEC-mediated mutagenesis induced by DNA repair acts downstream of the DNA repair pathways that generate the obligatory single-stranded substrates for TpC preferring APOBEC deaminases.
source: Figure 10 summarizes our results, which suggest that APOBEC-mediated mutagenesis induced by DNA repair acts downstream of the DNA repair pathways that generate the obligatory single-stranded substrates for TpC preferring APOBEC deaminases (Conticello et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is a summary inference from all the experimental data and supported by citation.

claim: Components of both BER and MMR are required to generate the deaminase substrates from both T/G and U/G.
source: siRNA knockdowns (bold font depicts the factors that we tested) indicate that components of both BER and MMR are required to generate the deaminase substrates from both T/G and U/G
evidence: This claim is supported by siRNA knockdown data in Figure 8.

claim: PCNA and ATR could modulate the availability of APOBEC substrates to the deaminases.
source: and that PCNA and ATR could modulate the availability of these substrates to the deaminases.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the knockdown data in Figure 9.

claim: MMR can hijack the 3′ end of the nick that would result from a U/G-BER intermediate and generate a single stranded region 5′ of the lesion that could serve as an APOBEC substrate.
source: With respect to U/G and T/G, we depict the interaction of the BER and MMR pathways in the framework of that proposed from elegant biochemical studies that showed that MMR can hijack the 3′ end of the nick that would result from a U/G-BER intermediate and generate a single stranded region 5′ of the lesion that could serve as an APOBEC substrate (Kadyrov et al., 2006; Schanz et al., 2009; Pluciennik et al., 2010; Peña-Diaz et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is based on citations to biochemical studies and used to interpret the current data.

claim: MMR could directly access T/G mismatches in a PCNA-dependent reaction.

source: some of our findings are at odds with the biochemical model—for example, the apparent inhibitory effect of PCNA on U/G-repair induced mutagenesis (knockdown increases its mutagenic effect, Figure 9) vs the requirement for PCNA in the MMR hijacking of BER (Kadyrov et al., 2006; Pluciennik et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is inferred from comparison of the current data with biochemical studies.

claim: The effects of knocking down various BER and MMR components, as well as the ATR and PCNA knockdowns distinguish the T/G- and U/G-repair intermediates.
source: while the effects of knocking down various BER and MMR components, as well as the ATR and PCNA knockdowns distinguish the T/G- and U/G-repair intermediates
evidence: This claim is inferred from the knockdown data.

claim: A migrating D-loop can be mounted on either strand of the episome to provide a top or bottom strand deaminase substrate.

source: Numerous recent studies support a role for the TpC preferring APOBEC C deaminases, especially APOBEC3B, in generating large numbers of mutations (i.e., the 'mutator phenotype' [Bielas et al., 2006; Venkatesan et al., 2006]) that characterize the progression, and perhaps initiation, of cancers (Nik-Zainal et al., 2012; Roberts et al., 2012; Stephens et al., 2012; Burns et al., 2013; Leonard et al., 2013; Roberts et al., 2013; Taylor et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to cancer genomics studies.

source: The hundreds of T/Gs and U/Gs that are generated daily by spontaneous hydrolytic deamination respectively of methyl-C and C would provide a continual source of potential APOBEC substrates.

source: This source could also be potentially augmented by the thousands of other BER-processed lesions that arise daily due to additional spontaneous degradative processes (Atamna et al., 2000; Barnes and Lindahl, 2004).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the current findings and supported by citations.

source: Additionally, the availability of APOBEC deaminases per se may not be sufficient to support repair-induced mutagenesis (Figure 7, also observed in certain cancers, Roberts et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 7 and citation.

claim: Some of the factors required to either generate APOBEC substrates from repair-intermediates, or recruit the deaminases to them, might not be present in all cells.
source: Thus some of the factors required to either generate APOBEC substrates from repair-intermediates, or recruit the deaminases to them, might not be present in all cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the cell line comparison data.

claim: Repair-associated mutagenesis might contribute to the genetic changes that underlie various disease states, aging and evolutionary change.
source: Repair-associated mutagenesis might not only contribute to the genetic changes that underlie various disease states (e.g., cancer, as discussed above) but also aging and evolutionary change (as has been earlier suggested, e.g., Huttley et al., 2000; Walser and Furano, 2010)
evidence: This claim is speculative and supported by citations to previous suggestions.

evidence: This claim is supported by unpublished data from the authors and citations.

claim: The normal cycling of the epigenetic methyl-C mark could contribute to the high mutation rate of regulatory sequences thought to contribute both disease processes and evolutionary novelty.
source: Thus, the normal cycling of the epigenetic methyl-C mark could contribute to the high mutation rate of regulatory sequences thought to contribute both disease processes (Maurano et al., 2012) and evolutionary novelty (Wittkopp and Kalay, 2012).
